howItWorks.intro: Your candy budget for Halloween comes down to a short chain of multiplication: how many trick-or-treaters show up, how many pieces each one gets, what those pieces cost per unit, and a safety buffer so you're not dark by 8 p.m. This calculator runs that exact chain using the same math a careful shopper would do with a receipt and a phone calculator, just instantly.
rules: Total Pieces = ⌈(Expected Trick-or-Treaters × Pieces per Child) × (1 + Buffer % ÷ 100)⌉ — rounded up to a whole piece
Candy Cost = Total Pieces × Cost per Piece, where the per-piece price follows your quality tier: Budget Mix $0.08, Name Brand Mix $0.15, Full-Size Bars $1.00, Premium/King-Size $1.50
Total Halloween Budget = Candy Cost + Decoration Budget
Cost per Trick-or-Treater = Candy Cost ÷ Expected Trick-or-Treaters

Bags to Buy = ⌈Total Pieces ÷ Pieces per Bag⌉, using 90 pieces per bag for Budget and Name Brand fun-size mixes and 18 pieces per bag for Full-Size or Premium bars — roughly how those products are actually packaged at retail
howItWorks.outro: These are planning numbers, not a guarantee. Rain, a competing block party, or a viral 'best house on the street' two doors down can swing real turnout by 30% or more in either direction, which is exactly why the buffer percentage exists. Note how many pieces you actually hand out this year and use that to dial in next Halloween's numbers.

faq.question: How many trick-or-treaters should I plan for?
faq.answer: It depends far more on walkability than on population. A rural home at the end of a driveway might see 5-15 kids all night, a typical suburban cul-de-sac or subdivision block sees 50-100, and a dense, well-decorated, or well-known street can pull 150-300+. If you don't have last year's count, ask a neighbor who's been there a few Halloweens, or start around 50-60 and lean on the buffer percentage to cover the uncertainty.

faq.question: What's the cheapest way to buy Halloween candy per piece?
faq.answer: Warehouse-club variety bags (Costco, Sam's Club, BJ's) typically run $0.06-$0.09 per piece for 200+ count bags — this calculator's Budget Mix tier. Grocery-store name-brand assortments (Hershey's, Mars, Reese's) run $0.13-$0.18 per piece, matching the Name Brand Mix tier. Full-size bars jump to roughly $0.75-$1.25 each since you're paying for a whole candy bar instead of a fun-size sliver, and premium or king-size bars run $1.25-$2. Moving from budget to name-brand roughly doubles your per-piece cost; moving to full-size multiplies it 7-10x.

faq.question: How many pieces come in a standard bag of Halloween candy?
faq.answer: Most 'family size' or 'party size' fun-size variety bags hold somewhere between 80 and 130 pieces, which is why this calculator assumes 90 pieces per bag for Budget and Name Brand mixes when estimating how many bags to buy. Full-size and premium/king-size bars are sold in smaller multi-packs, typically 12-24 count, so the calculator uses 18 pieces per bag for those two tiers. Always check the count on the actual bag — it varies by brand and by how deep the seasonal discount runs.

faq.question: Should I hand out full-size bars instead of fun-size?
faq.answer: Full-size bars make your house the one kids remember, but at roughly $1.00 per piece versus $0.15 for a name-brand fun-size mix, you're paying about 6-7x more per trick-or-treater. A common middle ground is giving full-size bars to the first 20-30 kids of the night, when energy and photos are highest, then switching to a fun-size backup once the bowl runs low. Run both quality tiers through this calculator with the same headcount to see the real dollar gap before deciding.

faq.question: When should I buy Halloween candy to get the best price?
faq.answer: Early-to-mid October usually has the best combination of full selection and pre-discount pricing. Prices dip again in the final week before Halloween as stores clear shelf space, but popular mixes sell out fast. The real bargain is November 1st, when post-Halloween clearance regularly runs 50-75% off — great for stocking up for next year, school parties, or baking, as long as you can keep it out of reach until then.

faq.question: What if I run out of candy before trick-or-treating ends?
faq.answer: That's exactly what the buffer percentage protects against — a 20% buffer on 80 expected kids adds 48 extra pieces for a few dollars, which is cheap insurance against going dark early. If you do run out, common fallbacks are non-candy treats you already have on hand (stickers, glow bracelets, juice boxes) or simply turning off the porch light, the universal signal you're done for the night. A realistic buffer up front is almost always cheaper than a last-minute store run.

howWeCalculate.intro: The calculator chains four pieces of shopping math together — the same math you'd do manually with a phone calculator and a bag's price tag, just automated so you can compare quality tiers and headcounts in seconds.
steps: Multiply Expected Trick-or-Treaters by Pieces per Child to get a base piece count — 80 kids at 3 pieces each is 240 pieces before any cushion.
Add the Extra Buffer percentage on top and round up to a whole piece, since candy doesn't split. A 20% buffer on 240 pieces brings the total to 288.

Multiply total pieces by the per-piece price tied to the chosen Candy Quality tier — Budget Mix at $0.08, Name Brand Mix at $0.15, Full-Size Bars at $1.00, or Premium/King-Size at $1.50 — to get Candy Cost.

Add the Decoration Budget to Candy Cost for Total Halloween Budget, divide Candy Cost by the trick-or-treater count for Cost per Trick-or-Treater, and divide total pieces by an assumed pieces-per-bag figure (90 for fun-size mixes, 18 for full-size/premium) to estimate Bags to Buy.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These are shopping-planning estimates based on typical retail pricing and packaging, not a quote from any specific store. Actual bag counts, weights, and prices vary by retailer, region, and how close to Halloween you're shopping — check the package before you check out.

sections.title: What the Halloween Candy Cost Calculator Does
sections.body: This calculator turns five decisions — expected trick-or-treaters, pieces per child, candy quality tier, decoration budget, and a safety buffer percentage — into a full Halloween spending picture. It returns total pieces needed, candy cost, a combined Total Halloween Budget (candy plus decorations), cost per trick-or-treater, and how many bags to actually buy. It's built around how candy is really priced and packaged: four quality tiers from $0.08 to $1.50 per piece, and bag sizes that mirror the shelf — about 90 pieces in a standard fun-size variety bag, closer to 18 in a full-size or premium multi-pack.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.body: Say you expect 80 trick-or-treaters, plan 3 pieces each, choose the Name Brand Mix at $0.15/piece, budget $50 for decorations, and add a 20% buffer. That's 80 × 3 = 240 base pieces; a 20% cushion brings it to 288. At $0.15 each, that's $43.20 in candy. Add the $50 decoration budget and Total Halloween Budget lands at $93.20, or about $0.54 per trick-or-treater. A standard fun-size variety bag holds around 90 pieces, so 288 pieces means 288 ÷ 90 = 3.2 bags — round up and buy 4. Switch the same headcount and buffer to Full-Size Bars at $1.00/piece instead, and candy cost jumps to $288 while, at roughly 18 bars per bag, you'd need 16 bags rather than 4.

sections.title: Why Real Halloween Spending Runs High or Low
sections.body: Two things blow up most Halloween candy budgets: underestimating turnout and buying the wrong package size for your quality tier. Turnout is driven more by walkability and reputation than raw population — a well-lit, decorated house on a short block with sidewalks can out-draw a bigger but spread-out neighborhood by 3-4x. That's what the buffer percentage guards against: a 20-25% cushion costs a few dollars but is the difference between handing out candy until 8:30 p.m. and going dark at 7. Package size matters too — full-size bars come in small 12-18 count boxes, so covering a large or unpredictable crowd means several separate purchases, while budget and name-brand fun-size mixes in 90-130 count bags scale far more cleanly. Testing a couple of quality-tier and buffer combinations before you shop is the fastest way to land on a bag count that neither leaves the porch dark early nor buries you in discounted candy corn on November 1st.

howToSteps.title: Enter Expected Trick-or-Treaters
howToSteps.description: Estimate how many kids will come to your door. Rural homes might see 10-20, typical suburban blocks see 50-100, and busy or well-decorated streets can pull 150+. When in doubt, check last year's leftover candy or ask a longtime neighbor.

howToSteps.title: Set Pieces per Child
howToSteps.description: Most households give 2-3 pieces per trick-or-treater. Fewer pieces stretch your budget across more kids; more pieces makes your house a standout stop but burns through inventory faster.

howToSteps.title: Choose Your Candy Quality
howToSteps.description: Pick Budget Mix ($0.08/piece), Name Brand Mix ($0.15/piece), Full-Size Bars ($1.00/piece), or Premium/King-Size ($1.50/piece). This single choice usually swings your total cost more than any other input.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Decoration Budget
howToSteps.description: Add what you plan to spend on pumpkins, lights, yard decor, or a fog machine. This is added to candy cost for one combined Total Halloween Budget.

howToSteps.title: Set Your Extra Buffer Percentage
howToSteps.description: Add a safety margin, typically 15-25%, to cover turnout running higher than expected. The buffer is cheap; running out of candy at dusk is not.

howToSteps.title: Click Calculate and Review Your Results
howToSteps.description: Check Total Pieces Needed, Candy Cost, Total Halloween Budget, Cost per Trick-or-Treater, and Bags to Buy. Adjust the quality tier or buffer and recalculate to compare scenarios before heading to the store.

tips: Buy variety bags from warehouse clubs for the lowest per-piece price — they typically beat individual grocery-store bags by 30-40% per piece.
Round your bag purchase up, not down. If the calculator says you need 3.2 bags, buy 4 — a spare bag costs a few dollars and covers higher-than-expected turnout.
Weigh full-size bars against fun-size mixes by cost per trick-or-treater, not cost per bag — full-size candy typically costs 6-10x more per piece.
Shop early-to-mid October for the best selection, but keep the bag sealed until closer to Halloween so you're not restocking your own candy bowl before trick-or-treaters arrive.
Track how many pieces you actually hand out this year and note it somewhere — it's the single best input for dialing in next year's Expected Trick-or-Treaters and buffer percentage.
